title: Talking Too Much: Where the Complaint Lands
core: All four cover the same raw fact: a person producing far more speech than the occasion requires. What separates them is not the word count but the angle of attack — whether the speaker is admiring the ease of the flow, dryly noting the excess, or complaining about being trapped. Three are adjectives labelling the talker; one is a verb naming the drift itself. The exam almost never tests "does this mean talkative"; it tests which shade of judgement the sentence has already set up.

words.nuance: The only one that is unambiguously a complaint, and the complaint is specifically about **triviality plus digression** — not just too much, but too much about nothing. Choose it when the sentence supplies a captive, suffering listener, or the classic subject (the old man, the seatmate, the barber).

Names quantity while withholding the verdict — the diction is arch enough to signal the speaker is being polite about it. Reach for **loquacious** when the sentence is amused or ironic rather than annoyed (*a loquacious witness*, *loquacious after two glasses*); the excess is noted, not indicted.

Measures **ease, not quantity** — the words arrive fluently, rapidly, with no groping or stalling. It is the only one of the four that can be straight praise (*a voluble advocate*), and the only one that fits a short, fast, perfectly on-point outpouring.

The verb for the *structural* failure: drifting off point, burying the thesis. It says nothing about volume or fluency, and it is never an accusation of error — a **rambling** answer is tiring, not wrong. Note the benign walking sense (a Sunday **ramble**), which the other three have no equivalent of.

exam_note: Sentence Equivalence loves pairing these as near-synonyms, then hinging the answer on a single clue word: "effortlessly"/"never hesitated" forces **voluble**, "tedious"/"about nothing at all" forces **garrulous**, "wandered from"/"never reached the point" forces **rambling** — and **loquacious** is the safe filler that only works when the sentence stays neutral.
